title: How Profiling Works
summary: Hosts open with Chuck announcing the birth of his daughter Ruby Rose and thanking people from their Tulsa stay, then turn to listener mail and the main topic: how profiling works in policing. They cover accepted forms (be-on-the-lookout descriptions, psychological profiling, predictive profiling), the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, Terry v. Ohio and articulable suspicion, cumulative similarities, US v. Sokolow, traffic stops and consent searches, drug dog sniffs and the 2015 Rodriguez-era limits on prolonged detention, racial profiling and its effectiveness, the New Jersey State Troopers case, post-9/11 airport profiling, and the 1972 Lod Airport attack. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a water slide mishap at Typhoon Lagoon.

segments.title: Chuck's baby announcement and Tulsa thanks
segments.summary: Chuck announces the birth of his daughter Ruby Rose, born on his birthday, and the hosts thank people who hosted them in Tulsa, Oklahoma, plus their caseworker and fans.

segments.title: Introduction to profiling and accepted forms
segments.summary: The hosts introduce profiling as a divisive topic and describe the accepted form of an all points bulletin, where a suspect description is based on eyewitness accounts after a crime.

segments.title: Psychological profiling
segments.summary: Psychological profiling is described as filling in gaps using crime scene clues when there is little physical evidence or no eyewitness, with the hosts noting it is a guessing game and comparing it with Sherlock Holmes.

segments.title: Predictive profiling and drug courier examples
segments.summary: Predictive profiling tries to anticipate crimes and is more controversial. The hosts describe a South Florida drug trafficking profile and note that a profile must be tied to a time and place to be justified.

segments.title: Terry stops, articulable suspicion and cumulative similarities
segments.summary: The hosts explain Terry v. Ohio and articulable suspicion, and the cumulative similarities approach attributed to Florida Highway Patrolman Bob Vogel, which combines many factors into a profile.

segments.title: Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments and probable cause
segments.summary: The hosts read the text of the Fourth Amendment and discuss probable cause, warrants, rubber-stamping, and how the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause relates to profiling.

segments.title: US v. Sokolow case
segments.summary: The hosts describe US v. Sokolow, in which a man at Honolulu airport carrying a kilo of cocaine was arrested based on a combination of travel behaviors; the Supreme Court found the totality of evidence sufficient.

segments.title: Traffic stops, consent searches and drug dogs
segments.summary: The hosts cover legal grounds for traffic stops, plain view, refusing consent to searches, detention while waiting for canine units, and a recent Supreme Court ruling limiting prolonged detention for drug dog sniffs. Chuck shares a story of being searched in Texas.

segments.title: Racial profiling debate and effectiveness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss racial profiling, arguments on both sides using the same statistics, the view of a former Palo Alto police chief that it is ineffective and lazy policing, the New Jersey State Troopers case, state anti-profiling laws, and post-9/11 airport profiling including the Lod Airport attack.

segments.title: Listener mail: water slide mishap
segments.summary: Listener Tiffany describes an embarrassing accident on the Cowabunga water slide at Typhoon Lagoon at Disney World as an eleven year old. The hosts close with listener contact information.
